difficultyReason: Requires chaining three facts (antibody prevalence, post-exposure infection rate, severity finding) and recognizing a tension between high exposure and mild outcomes to support a hedged claim about protective factors. Trap (B) overreaches from 'some' to 'most'; trap (D) points opposite to what the severity data imply.
stimulus: In a community where a newly identified respiratory virus circulated last winter, serological testing later revealed that more than 70 percent of adult residents had been exposed to the virus at some point during the season. Yet the local clinic recorded confirmed symptomatic infections in only about a quarter of the adult population. Of the symptomatic cases that were recorded, those in residents who had received the previous season's standard influenza vaccine were, on average, markedly milder than those in unvaccinated residents, even though the new virus is not closely related to any influenza strain.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some adult residents exposed to the new virus had some immune response that either prevented symptomatic infection or reduced its severity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most adult residents of the community who were exposed to the new virus experienced no symptoms at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The previous season's influenza vaccine confers specific immunity against the newly identified respiratory virus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residents who received the previous season's influenza vaccine were more likely to become symptomatically infected with the new virus than unvaccinated residents were.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The newly identified respiratory virus is less dangerous than the influenza strains targeted by the previous season's vaccine.

explanations.correct: Three facts combine: exposure was widespread (over 70%), symptomatic infection was far less common (about a quarter), and among those who were symptomatic, prior flu-vaccine recipients had milder illness. Together they support the hedged claim that at least some exposed residents had an immune response that either blocked symptoms or dampened them. 'At least some' and 'either...or' match what the data can carry.
explanations.B: Too strong and slightly off-scope — the stimulus gives community-wide exposure and symptomatic rates but not the specific fraction of exposed residents who were asymptomatic; 'most' is not warranted, and the stimulus speaks to recorded symptomatic cases, not a clean asymptomatic tally.
explanations.C: Too strong — milder severity in vaccinated residents is consistent with nonspecific immune effects; 'confers specific immunity' overreaches.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the severity finding suggests vaccinated residents fared better, not worse.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — no comparison of the new virus's overall danger to influenza strains is given.

difficultyReason: Must integrate three qualifications — effort-level reporting, confidence ratings, and the subgroup reversal — to support a hedged claim about the relationship between overconfidence and actual performance. Trap (C) treats a comparative as absolute; trap (E) drops the effort qualification.
stimulus: In a large study of undergraduates preparing for standardized exams, students who reported studying fewer than ten hours per week rated themselves, on average, more confident about their readiness than students who reported studying twenty or more hours per week. On the exam itself, the high-study group outperformed the low-study group by a substantial margin. However, within the low-study group, those students who had rated themselves least confident scored about as well as the average student in the high-study group.
questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Among students who study relatively little, those who are less confident about their readiness tend to perform better on the exam than their more confident peers in the same study-hours group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Confidence about readiness is a more reliable predictor of exam performance than reported study hours are.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any student who studies twenty or more hours per week will score higher on the exam than any student who studies fewer than ten.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students tend to overestimate how much time they actually spend studying for standardized exams.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students who rate themselves least confident about their readiness will score about as well as students who study twice as many hours.

explanations.correct: Within the low-study group, the least-confident subset matched the average of the high-study group, while the low-study group on the whole trailed the high-study group. That subgroup reversal supports the hedged claim that, within the low-study group, lower confidence tracks with stronger performance. 'Tend to' respects the averaging in the data.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus gives no direct comparison of predictive reliability across the two variables.
explanations.C: Absolute claim from comparative data — the stimulus reports group averages, not per-individual guarantees.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus uses reported study hours and does not address their accuracy.
explanations.E: Drops the crucial qualifier that the match holds for the least-confident students within the low-study group; the inference would be stronger and misapplied as stated.

difficultyReason: Requires chaining the rainfall datum, the staple-crop yield, and the household-garden finding to support a hedged inference about crop mix. Trap (B) is the plausible-but-unsupported worldly truth; trap (D) inverts the direction by treating the overall decline as uniform.
stimulus: Data from agricultural monitoring stations in the semi-arid province of Marenda show that the past decade has been, on average, the driest of any decade since record-keeping began. Overall yields of the province's main staple crop, sorghum, have declined by roughly 15 percent relative to the previous decade. However, yields from small household gardens in the same region, in which farmers typically plant a mix of drought-tolerant vegetables alongside smaller amounts of sorghum, have held roughly steady over the same period.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some agricultural plots in Marenda have been less affected by the decade's drier conditions than the province's overall sorghum yield would suggest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Household gardens are generally more productive per unit of land than commercial sorghum fields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If commercial farms in Marenda shifted entirely away from sorghum to drought-tolerant vegetables, their yields would rise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All sorghum plots in Marenda have shown comparable declines in yield over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rainfall is the only agricultural factor that has changed in Marenda over the past decade.

explanations.correct: Overall sorghum yields fell by about 15 percent as conditions grew drier, yet household gardens — which mix drought-tolerant vegetables with smaller amounts of sorghum — held steady. That supports the hedged claim that some plots have been less affected than the headline sorghum figure suggests. The inference chains three facts without overreaching.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — productivity per unit of land isn't established; the stimulus compares yield changes, not absolute productivity.
explanations.C: Too strong — a full shift of commercial farms is a policy prediction the stimulus does not support.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the household-garden finding shows not all plots declined uniformly.
explanations.E: Too strong — the stimulus notes dry conditions but does not rule out other changes.

difficultyReason: Must chain the settlement statistic, the docket-composition datum, and the contingency-fee observation, recognizing the tension between case mix and outcome mix, to support a hedged claim about plaintiff representation. Trap (A) overreaches to 'more skilled'; trap (C) mis-scopes the plaintiff-defendant comparison.
stimulus: A recent review of civil cases filed in the Hargreave County trial court found that cases in which the plaintiff was represented by an attorney settled before trial roughly twice as often as cases in which the plaintiff appeared without counsel. The review also found that represented plaintiffs' cases disproportionately involved claims for which attorneys are willing to work on contingency — that is, claims with a relatively high expected monetary value. Among cases that were not settled and went to trial, represented and unrepresented plaintiffs prevailed at similar rates.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attorneys who represent plaintiffs in Hargreave County are, on average, more skilled at litigation than attorneys who represent defendants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The higher settlement rate among represented plaintiffs is likely due at least in part to features of their cases other than the quality of their representation at trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plaintiffs without counsel in Hargreave County win at trial more often than defendants without counsel do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any plaintiff who retains an attorney in Hargreave County is more likely to receive a monetary award than one who does not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attorneys working on contingency refuse to take cases unless a pretrial settlement is likely.

explanations.correct: Three facts: represented plaintiffs settle about twice as often; their cases disproportionately involve high-value, contingency-eligible claims; yet at trial, represented and unrepresented plaintiffs prevail at similar rates. The similar trial-win rates tug against a pure 'lawyering makes plaintiffs win' story, and the case-mix fact offers another driver. Together these support the hedged claim that the settlement gap is at least partly due to non-trial-quality features of the cases themselves.
explanations.A: Out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about defense attorneys' skill.
explanations.C: Mis-scoped — unrepresented defendants are not addressed.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'any' and 'more likely' extrapolate beyond averages and ignore the similar trial-win finding.
explanations.E: Too strong — contingency-fee behavior is described only as a pattern, not as a rigid refusal rule.

difficultyReason: Requires integrating the subscription data, the reading-time finding, and the recall-score result to recognize a tension between volume consumed and retention. Trap (E) is a plausible worldly truth; trap (B) overreaches from 'some' to 'most'.
stimulus: A survey of readers of general-interest news publications found that subscribers to a high-volume daily news service reported, on average, consuming more articles per week than subscribers to a weekly news digest. The daily-service subscribers also reported spending, on average, less time per article than the digest subscribers did. When both groups were asked a week later to recall substantive details from articles they had read during the survey period, digest subscribers scored noticeably higher than daily-service subscribers on recall of policy-oriented articles, while the two groups scored comparably on recall of articles about entertainment.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reading a larger number of news articles per week tends to improve a reader's retention of details from those articles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most daily-service subscribers would retain more policy-oriented details if they spent more time per article.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For at least some categories of news, the amount of time spent per article is more closely associated with retention than is the sheer number of articles read.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Digest subscribers are, on the whole, more interested in policy issues than daily-service subscribers are.

choices.label: E
choices.text: News services that deliver fewer but longer articles should be preferred by readers who want to stay informed.

explanations.correct: Digest subscribers read fewer articles but spent more time per article; their recall of policy articles exceeded that of daily-service subscribers, though entertainment recall was comparable. This supports a hedged, category-scoped claim: for at least some kinds of news (policy), time-per-article tracks with retention more closely than article count does. The 'at least some categories' hedge and 'more closely associated' match what the data carry.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — daily-service subscribers read more articles but recalled less in the policy category.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'most' and 'would retain more' make a counterfactual and universal claim the data do not reach.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — no interest data are reported; the stimulus gives only recall scores.
explanations.E: Normative overreach — the stimulus does not license a recommendation about which service readers 'should' prefer.

difficultyReason: Must chain three ethical-practice facts — the nondisclosure rate, the patient-preference survey, and the follow-up finding — to support a hedged claim about the gap between professed preferences and realized outcomes. Trap (A) overreaches; trap (D) relies on a misreading of which group showed the follow-up effect.
stimulus: In a survey of physicians practicing in a large urban hospital system, roughly a third reported that they had at some point declined to disclose a minor error to a patient when they believed the error had caused no lasting harm. A separate survey of patients of the same system found that an overwhelming majority said they would want to be told of any error affecting their care, even if the error caused no lasting harm. A follow-up study found that patients who had later learned of an undisclosed minor error expressed, on average, only modestly lower trust in their physician than patients who had been promptly informed of a comparable error.
questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some physicians in the hospital system are not currently meeting the disclosure preferences of the patients they treat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients in the hospital system have at some point been the subject of an undisclosed minor medical error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promptly disclosing minor errors to patients maximally preserves patients' trust in their physicians.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who learn belatedly of an undisclosed error lose trust in their physicians as sharply as patients who are told promptly would have.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physicians who withhold disclosure of minor errors do so primarily out of concern for preserving patient trust.

explanations.correct: A third of physicians have at some point withheld disclosure of a minor error; an overwhelming majority of patients say they would want to be told of any error. That gap supports the hedged claim that at least some physicians are not meeting their patients' stated disclosure preferences. 'At least some' fits comfortably within the reported figures.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus gives the physician side ('at some point' withheld) and a preference survey, not the share of patients who have been affected.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'maximally preserves' is a superlative the follow-up study does not establish.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the follow-up found only modestly lower trust among those who learned belatedly.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — physicians' reasons for nondisclosure are not described.

difficultyReason: Requires chaining the pricing rule, the sales pattern, and the restocking observation to infer a hedged claim about demand in a specific category. Trap (B) is stimulus-neutral plausibility; trap (E) reverses direction by assuming the pattern generalizes.
stimulus: An online retailer adjusts prices on many items daily according to an automated algorithm that raises a listed item's price whenever the number of units sold in the previous 24 hours exceeds a threshold. Records show that over the past year the algorithm raised the price of a popular model of wireless headphones roughly three times as often as it raised the price of a competing model from the same manufacturer, even though the two models were initially listed at the same price. Staff also reported restocking the first model noticeably more often than the second during the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first model of wireless headphones was, over the past year, in greater demand at the retailer than the competing model was.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first model of wireless headphones is of higher quality than the competing model.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The retailer's pricing algorithm raises prices only for items whose sales exceed the threshold on several consecutive days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first model of wireless headphones is now priced considerably higher than the competing model.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any item whose price is raised three times as often as another item's price must be restocked three times as often as well.

explanations.correct: The algorithm raises prices when daily unit sales exceed a threshold; the first model's price was raised about three times as often as the competing model's, and staff restocked it noticeably more often. Together these facts support the hedged claim that the first model was in greater demand at this retailer over the year. 'Greater demand' is scoped to this retailer and this period, matching the evidence.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — quality is not addressed; demand could reflect branding, promotion, or other factors.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'only' and 'several consecutive days' add conditions not stated.
explanations.D: Too strong — more frequent price increases don't guarantee the current listed price is considerably higher; prices can also fall.
explanations.E: Too strong — the inference overgeneralizes the relationship between price increases and restocking frequency.

difficultyReason: Requires chaining emission, air-quality, and hospitalization data while recognizing the juxtaposition between lower emissions and stable hospitalizations to support a hedged claim about non-local pollution sources. Trap (A) flips direction; trap (C) over-applies the air-quality finding.
stimulus: Since the city of Polford adopted stricter emission limits on its municipal power plants a decade ago, measured emissions of fine particulate matter from those plants have declined by nearly half. Air-quality monitoring stations in residential neighborhoods near the plants have recorded only a modest improvement in average particulate levels during the same period. Hospital admissions in Polford for conditions linked to airborne particulates have remained roughly constant.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The stricter emission limits imposed on Polford's municipal power plants have caused residential air-quality monitors to record a sharp improvement in particulate levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sources of airborne particulates other than Polford's municipal power plants are likely contributing substantially to the particulate levels measured in Polford's residential neighborhoods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Particulate pollution is no longer a significant contributor to hospital admissions in Polford.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Emission limits similar to those adopted by Polford would fail to improve air quality in any city that adopted them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residents of neighborhoods near Polford's power plants have become less likely to seek hospital care for airborne-particulate-related conditions.

explanations.correct: Plant emissions fell by nearly half, yet residential particulate levels improved only modestly and hospitalizations were roughly constant. The gap between a large emissions drop and a small air-quality change supports the hedged claim that other sources are likely contributing substantially to local particulate levels. 'Likely' and 'substantially' fit the data without overreaching.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — the stimulus reports only a modest improvement in monitoring stations' readings.
explanations.C: Too strong — roughly constant admissions do not show particulates are no longer a significant contributor.
explanations.D: Too strong — a universal failure claim goes well beyond one city's experience.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — admissions rates in specific neighborhoods are not broken out.

difficultyReason: Chains the playwright's output pattern, the revival-frequency data, and the critical-reception datum, with a tension between later popularity and earlier acclaim. Trap (A) misreads 'among the most' as 'the most'; trap (D) drops the revival qualifier.
stimulus: A comprehensive survey of twentieth-century theater records shows that the playwright Helena Orsi produced more than forty full-length plays during her career. Of these, only eight have been professionally revived more than twice since her death, and nearly all of those eight premiered during the first decade of her career. Contemporary reviewers of Orsi's later-career plays had, on average, praised them more highly than her early-career plays, describing several as among the most formally inventive works of their decade.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The most formally inventive of Helena Orsi's plays is one of the eight that have been revived more than twice since her death.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Plays that are highly praised by contemporary reviewers tend to be revived more frequently after the playwright's death than plays that are not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frequency of posthumous professional revival and contemporary critical praise do not always track each other closely in the case of Helena Orsi's work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Helena Orsi's early-career plays have been revived more often than her later-career plays.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Critics in Helena Orsi's later career systematically overrated her work.

explanations.correct: Nearly all of Orsi's frequently revived plays premiered in her first decade, yet her later-career plays received, on average, higher critical praise, with several described as among the most formally inventive of their decade. That juxtaposition supports the hedged claim that, in Orsi's case, revival frequency and critical praise do not always track each other closely. 'Not always' and 'closely' are appropriately hedged.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'among the most formally inventive' does not single out one play, and the stimulus describes several later works that way.
explanations.B: Opposite direction — the Orsi data run the other way: more-praised later plays were revived less often.
explanations.D: Correct reading but extrapolated — we know nearly all of the frequently revived plays are early ones, but not the aggregate revival counts across eras; the stronger comparative may not hold.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — 'systematically overrated' imputes a critical failure the stimulus does not establish.

difficultyReason: Requires integrating the bandwidth-throttling policy, the queueing observation, and the peak-hour latency figure to support a hedged claim about a bottleneck's location. Trap (B) overreaches from 'some evidence' to 'primary cause'; trap (D) misreads the throttling condition.
stimulus: A regional internet service provider implemented a policy in which residential connections whose monthly traffic exceeds a threshold are throttled to a lower speed until the next billing cycle. Network engineers have observed that during peak evening hours, outbound queues at the provider's core routers fill up more quickly than at any other time, even though total traffic during peak hours is only modestly greater than at late-morning hours. Average latency measured at customer endpoints rises sharply during peak evening hours, including for customers whose connections are not being throttled.
questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some of the peak-hour latency experienced by the provider's customers is due to conditions at the provider's core routers rather than to the throttling policy alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The throttling policy is the primary cause of the elevated latency that customers experience during peak evening hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eliminating the throttling policy would substantially reduce average peak-hour latency for the provider's customers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every customer whose monthly traffic exceeds the threshold experiences higher average latency than every customer whose traffic does not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Expanding capacity at the core routers would eliminate peak-hour latency for all of the provider's customers.

explanations.correct: Core-router outbound queues fill up fastest during peak evening hours despite only modestly higher traffic than late morning, and peak-hour latency rises sharply even for non-throttled customers. Together these support the hedged claim that at least some of the peak-hour latency comes from conditions at the core routers, not only from the throttling policy. 'At least some' and 'rather than...alone' fit the data.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'primary cause' goes beyond what the non-throttled latency rise supports; it is evidence against sole-cause attribution, not for primary attribution.
explanations.C: Too strong — a counterfactual policy prediction not established by the data.
explanations.D: Mis-scoped — the stimulus does not give a throttled-versus-non-throttled latency comparison across all customers.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'eliminate...for all' overreaches from a contributing-cause inference.
